{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the lower tail early (stroke 4) and had it live to the tip. I then built the back half of the body lines coming forward from the crossing, and I made the join to Maya's bottom line in the middle. These pieces carried a large share of the fish's outline, including the tail fork that makes it read as a fish. In the last minutes I lifted the pale stray dominoes past the tail so they went back to the pile for the notch join.

Execution: I worked methodically on the fiddly parts. I laid the tail, extended lines from their ends, and connected the body to the crossing in sequence. I inspected the notch and tail area repeatedly, so the table knew which pieces were live and which were open. I cleared the jams on the upper tail and stood back up the dominoes that needed it. I finished before the clock ran out.

Collaboration: I told the table what I was building and where my line ended. I asked Maya and Priya to say where they'd stopped so I could make the joins, and I left the notch alone while Maya worked there so our hands didn't collide. I answered Tom's request to check the upper tail tip with a clear read of what was still open. I also sent my freed-up dominoes to Maya when the pile ran low.

Leadership: I kept the join points visible to everyone. I flagged the crossing and the notch as the places a break could hide, and I split the remaining jobs so people weren't working on top of each other. With two minutes left I asked for the status of the last join and said exactly what I would fix once the space was clear. I took ownership of the lower tail and the body-to-crossing connections and delivered both.", "my_share_percent": 28}
